title: Smarter Than Us
subtitle: The Rise of Machine Intelligence
pitch: A short, sharp introduction by an Oxford researcher: why telling a superintelligence what we want is much harder than it sounds.

chapters.g: Forget killer robots. The real danger is a very capable system doing exactly what it was told.
Intelligence, not strength, is what made humans dominant.

chapters.t: What is intelligence? Can we achieve it artificially?
chapters.g: A working definition of intelligence and why machines could have it.
Copying, speed and scale could make AI very powerful very fast.
An AI's mind would not be like ours, so communicating goals is hard.

chapters.t: Our values are complex and fragile
chapters.g: Leave out one thing we care about and the result could be a disaster.

chapters.t: What, precisely, do we really (really) want?
chapters.g: Even we do not know exactly what we want.

chapters.t: We need to get it all exactly right
chapters.g: Why near misses are not good enough with a superintelligence.

chapters.t: Listen to the sound of absent experts
chapters.g: Why expert opinion on AI timelines is less reliable than it seems.
What readers can do to help.

ideas: The danger is competence plus wrong goals, not evil robots.
Human values are complex and fragile.
We have to specify goals almost exactly right.

args.a: Getting values exactly right is necessary.
args.c: Approaches like corrigibility and AI control aim to stay safe even if values are not perfect.

questions: Try writing down exactly what you want an AI to do for humanity. What goes wrong?

quiz.q: What does Armstrong say is the real danger?
o: A capable AI following goals that are slightly wrong
quiz.w: Competence plus imperfect goals is the problem.
